_comment: Levelling: what a kill is worth in experience, what a level costs, and
what one point buys in each attribute. game/progression.py
holds the arithmetic and none of the values.
*** THIS SYSTEM SHIPS SWITCHED OFF. xp_base IS ZERO. ***
Nothing is earned, no level is ever reached, the panel never opens and
every attribute in the game resolves to neutral -- which is what makes the
recorded 280-cell class-by-stage grid provably unmoved by the whole
attribute layer, rather than unmoved as far as anybody has checked.
test_neutral_attributes_reproduce_todays_arithmetic settles that in
milliseconds; tools/balance.py would take minutes and prove less.
Setting xp_base back to 0 is also the rollback, exactly as gold.base and
item_chance are for the loot layer. The code goes quiet without being
removed.
BEFORE TURNING IT ON, read the note on `allocate` in game/autoplay.py.
The reference bot presses the light attack and spends nothing. A player
always spends levels -- unlike gold, there is no reason not to -- so a
sweep run against an unlevelled hero measures a game nobody plays and
reports it in the same units as difficulty. That is the flanker demon
again: an instrument without the behaviour cannot measure the feature.
Teach autoplay to allocate first, then re-baseline the grid, and treat
every number below as a guess until that has happened.
_xp_comment: xp = xp_base * monster_level. The same shape as the gold formula and
deliberately reusing the same input: EntityType.level already means 'how
dangerous was that', it is already tuned, and inventing a second danger
scale beside it is two dials doing one job.
No floor multiplier here, unlike gold. Depth already pays through the
roster -- act VIII fields level 9-12 creatures where act I fields level
1-2 -- so a second multiplier on top would compound into the hero
out-levelling the campaign somewhere around act VI.
Draws no dice. A kill is worth exactly what the table says, so the
progression layer touches none of the three RNG streams and cannot
disturb a damage roll however it is tuned.

_comment: Cost of the Nth level is first + step * (N - 1), so levels 2, 3 and 4
cost 60, 105 and 150. Linear rather than exponential: the campaign is
forty stages of roughly rising value, and a curve that bends the other
way would put every level in the first act or every level in the last.
max_level caps the total spend at 19 levels x 3 points = 57 points.
That number is the whole budget the attribute values below are drafted
against, and it is a guess until a sweep says otherwise.
What one point buys, in each attribute's own units -- flat for the
first three, per-mille for crit and evasion, hundredths of a hit point
per tick for regen.
ALL SEVEN ARE UNMEASURED FIRST-PASS GUESSES. They are drafted against
the recorded shape of the game rather than against a sweep:
max_hp 4   -- 57 points is +228, near double a Knight's 130. The cap
is doing the work here, not this number.
damage 1   -- flat, because the classes are an order of magnitude
apart per swing (rogue dagger 5, magician bolt 15) and a
percentage would pay the magician three times over.
defense 1  -- the most dangerous dial in the file. A rogue's 5-damage
dagger against 4 defense is a 60% cut, and MIN_DAMAGE
then floors every hit at 1, which is how a stage runs to
the tick limit and reports as a balance failure. Enemy
defense is 0 everywhere on purpose; see entities.json.
crit 15/25 -- 20 points is a 30% rate; 20 more is +50% damage on it.
evasion 8  -- deliberately the meanest of them all. See below.
regen 5    -- 10 points is one hit point every two seconds, which is
about a third of a Knight's between-stage heal over a
median stage.
move_speed 5 -- per-mille, so a point is +0.5% and the 57-point budget
is +28.5%. Priced under the Boots in the shop (+5% a
pair, four pairs) on purpose: the shop good is the one a
player reaches for, and two systems selling the same
stat should not both be the cheap way to buy it.
Walking only -- the dodge roll's distance is fixed. See
sim._walk_speed.
On evasion specifically: docs/design.md opens by saying that taking a
hit is a decision you made rather than something the arena did to you.
A random miss is precisely the arena doing something to you, in both
directions, so it is priced to be a garnish rather than a build. It is
the attribute most likely to be cut outright once somebody plays it.
